title: Facing prejudice
hook: meeting hostility with dignity and courage
tomorrow: Simran has to tell her side at school. what about the fear?

segments.voice: Yesterday, stand up: see the wrong, stand beside the person, name it, peacefully first. Simran did. Now someone has come after her.

By lunch, an account with no face has left a comment under Simran's bus stop video: go back home. She was born two towns over. Her thumbs are already typing something she'd regret. Then a text from her dad, Harjit, who hears worse at truck stops: before you answer, read Ang 1293. So she does, and finds something odd. Right there in the Guru Granth Sahib, a poet tells everyone the exact thing people used to look down on him for. He doesn't hide it. He puts it in a hymn. Why would anyone write the insult into scripture?
screen: `GO BACK HOME.` → `READ ANG 1293 FIRST.` → `A POET NAMES WHAT THEY MOCKED.` → `WHY WRITE THAT INTO SCRIPTURE?`

segments.voice: The poet is Bhagat Ravidas. In Sikh tradition he was a leatherworker, born into a family others of his time treated as untouchable. His hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own. On Ang 1293 he says, in paraphrase: my people carried dead cattle around Benares every day. Now even the leading Brahmins bow to them, because Ravidas has taken shelter in your Name. So here's the puzzle solved. He doesn't argue with the label, and he doesn't shrink from it either. He says it plainly, in the open, and then stands on something the label can't touch: the Name. That's dignity. Not pretending the word didn't land. Not snarling back. Just refusing to let someone else's word decide who you are. The detail to tell a friend tonight: a man people wouldn't share a well with is sung in gurdwaras, in his own words. Harjit's version is smaller. At a fuel stop once, a man told him to go home. Harjit smiled and said: I am home. Drive safe. Simran deletes her draft. She types three words under the video, I am home, and puts the phone face down.
screen: `RAVIDAS NAMES HIS OWN PEOPLE.` · `HE STANDS ON THE NAME.` · `DIGNITY: THEIR WORD ISN'T YOURS.` · `I AM HOME. DRIVE SAFE.` · then, large: `DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand tall: feet flat, shoulders down, chin level, hands open. Let one label someone once put on you come to mind, and keep the posture anyway. With each slow breath, let the word be there without letting it bend your spine.
Facing prejudice. Meeting hostility with dignity: saying who you are plainly, and standing on something their words can't reach.
The line for today: dignity, the way Ravidas named his people and stood on the Name. Three words under a video, and the phone face down.

options: not soft. like Ravidas, you said who you are and stood on it.

chat.meaning: Ravidas names his people plainly and stands on the Name. Dignity isn't roasting back or hiding; it's not letting their word decide who you are.

Ravidas.meaning: a saint-poet whose hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib

Bhagat.meaning: a saint-poet, not one of the Gurus, whose hymns are in the Granth

Benares.meaning: an old holy city on the Ganges, also called Varanasi

Brahmins.meaning: the priestly caste, at the top of the old caste order

Ang 1293.meaning: the page of the Guru Granth Sahib with Ravidas's hymn
